slides.heading: What is in this lesson, and why it matters
body: Two consonants, one vowel.
One habit of the voice.
Three real Thai words.
Many consonants share a sound. Their **class** is what separates them.

slides.heading: The loops are your friends
body: **ชอบกินข้าวที่บ้านมาก** — six ordinary words, run together with no spaces.
Thai script looks like squiggles and loops.
The loops are your friends. They tell you where the pen goes down.
slides.thai: ชอบกินข้าวที่บ้านมาก

slides.heading: There is a right way to write every symbol
body: Every symbol has a **stroke order** — a right way to write it.
Almost all are one continuous stroke, pen never lifted.
**Cheat code one:** start at the loop, if there is one.
The starting loop is called the **head**.
**ชอบกินข้าวที่บ้านมาก** — you'll read, say and write this yourself before the end.
slides.thai: ชอบกินข้าวที่บ้านมาก

slides.heading: Which way the loop turns
body: Some loops go **clockwise**, others **counter-clockwise**.
Some characters differ *only* in that.
Most symbols turn **clockwise**. Less than half as many go the other way.
**Cheat code two:** assume clockwise, and learn only the exceptions.

slides.heading: Every letter has a two-part name
body: Every letter's name has **two parts**.
Catch the sound at the front. The rest never changes.
First part = **the consonant sound plus one fixed vowel**, the one in "awe".
In English it would be **Saw**, **Paw**, **Jaw**.

slides.heading: And the second part is the NATO alphabet
body: Many consonants share a sound, so the name needs a second half.
That half is an everyday word starting with that sound.
Exactly like Alpha, Bravo, Charlie — built into the alphabet itself.
The alphabet song is a list of these words. It teaches no shapes.

slides.heading: Why that turns into a superpower here
body: Each letter comes attached to a **word**.
We put those words in **places**, and build stories there.
The place quietly teaches the grammar. And you get 44 free words.
Loops, stroke order and the naming system — all paid for once.

slides.heading: Your first consonant, and what alive means
body: The Thai version of **M**.
Close your lips and hum through your nose.
You already own this sound.
**Alive** — a sound you can hold as long as you have breath.

slides.heading: Its name, and how to use what comes next
body: Its name: the hum plus the fixed vowel, then a word.
That word means **horse**.
Listen to the name. You will write it shortly.
Do not follow the story. Stand inside it.

slides.heading: The woman who fished from horseback
body: A woman who fished from horseback, out in the shallows.
No boat. Just the grey horse and a net.
Nobody could talk her out of it.

slides.heading: The boy on the dock
body: From the dock the boy could see the fish; she could not.
He shouted to point the way.
"Mom!" wore down to "Ma!"

slides.heading: The whole harbour knew that sound
body: The whole harbour knew that sound, and what it meant.
Between them they out-fished everyone.
The arguing stopped. It became the ordinary shape of the morning.

slides.heading: The morning she went out alone
body: One morning the boy was not on the dock.
She went out alone.
A wave came in off the ocean. Afterwards there was only water.

slides.heading: The horse came back
body: The horse came out of the surf alone.
The net still tangled around its legs.
It stopped in front of the boy. She was not there.

slides.heading: He kept calling
body: He called from the end of the pier. "Ma!" And again.
Nothing came back.
The horse went out every day for weeks, looking for her.

slides.heading: What the harbour left there
body: A wooden horse stands where the pier runs out, worn pale by hands.
Fishermen still touch its shoulder on the way out.
A brass plaque on its flank, with one word on it.

slides.heading: Come back out of it
body: The end of the pier, the wooden horse, the plaque.
That is the letter's address.
A place you have stood in, with something you can put your hand on.

slides.heading: The horse's letter
body: The horse's letter.
Find the **head** in the upper left, then follow the stroke down.

slides.heading: Stop here and fetch a pen
body: Real paper. A real pen.
Your hand learns a shape your eye only recognises.
Pause the lesson. Go and get them.

slides.heading: Now write it, and keep writing it
body: Start at the head, upper left. Loop **clockwise**.
Straight down. Second loop at the bottom.
Across, then straight up. One continuous stroke.
It will look wrong for a while. Fill the line anyway.
Write it again and again, saying both halves of its name.

slides.heading: Your second consonant
body: The Thai version of **N**. Tongue to the ridge behind your top teeth.
You can hold it, so it is **alive** — like the first one.
No puff of air after it.
The same two-part pattern as the first letter.

slides.heading: The net-mender who worked in the dark
body: An old net-mender, blind, working by touch.
Her son away at sea for a long season.
She wanted to know how long — and could not see to count.

slides.heading: Counting out loud in the dark
body: Her son left a knotted cord. One knot for each night away.
She untied one every night and hummed her way down what was left.
Mouth open, tongue behind the top teeth. That hum is the letter.

slides.heading: Her nocturnal, notorious, knot-nibbling neighbour
body: A mouse in the post, and she knew it: her **n**octurnal, **n**otorious, **k**not-**n**ibbling **n**eighbour.
It lives at this end of the quay because of the **snake** in the rope locker on the pier.
It wanted the rope fibre for its nest, and undid knots faster than she did.
She could not see. She could never prove it.

slides.heading: The night the cord ran out
body: Her fingers found the bare end, weeks too early.
Nothing left to count, so the humming stopped.
She sat in the doorway for days, believing the worst.

slides.heading: And then his boat came in
body: He came in on the night he had always said.
Her son found the nest in the post, lined with her stolen count.
That doorpost is where this letter lives.

slides.heading: The mouse's letter, and the stroke that makes it
body: The mouse's letter.
Head at the upper left, clockwise, then straight down.
Second loop thrown out to the **bottom right**.
Write it out, saying its name every time.

slides.heading: Two loops, and where the second one lands
body: Both open with the same **head**, high left. Nearly every Thai consonant does.
**ม** — second loop drops **straight down the left**. Stacked.
**น** — second loop thrown **across to the bottom right**. A diagonal.

slides.prompt: Both letters carry a head high on the left. Where does each one put its *second* loop — and which of the two is the horse?

slides.heading: Where these two letters live
body: Every consonant belongs to one of three **classes**.
The class decides the tone. That is the engine of the whole system.
Both of today's letters are in the same class — the **harbour**.
The rules themselves arrive next lesson.

slides.heading: One place, and everything in it
body: Both of today's letters are **low class**.
In this course, low class is the **harbour**.
The place is the class. The class decides the tone.

slides.heading: And one place that is not a district
body: A vowel carries no class, so it belongs to no district.
One house, where the roads from all three districts meet.
The room it lodges in is simply **where it is written**.

slides.heading: The vowel you have already heard
body: A **long**, open note, held until the breath runs out.
Vowel names are two parts too — but the front is always **สระ *sara***, meaning *vowel*.
So **สระอา** is simply *Vowel aa*.
Length changes meaning. Long and short are different vowels.
It is written **after** its consonant, so it lodges in the **back yard**.

slides.heading: What lodges in the back yard
body: The **dipper** by the water jar: a small crook at the top, then a long straight handle.
It hangs round the **back** of the house — where this vowel is written.
Tip it over your neck and you make the sound. Long, open, until the water stops.

slides.heading: Write the vowel
body: No loop, so no head — one of the exceptions.
One stroke: a small turn at the top, then straight down.
It always sits to the **right** of its consonant.

slides.heading: One rule about your own voice
body: Every syllable carries a **tone**, and the tone is part of the word.
Everything today is **flat and level**, halfway up your range.
Fight the English habit of rising for a question or falling to end.
Why they are flat is next lesson's whole subject.

slides.heading: Your first word
body: The mouse's letter, then the long vowel.
It means a **rice field** — and from now on it names the flat field where your mid tones live.
Consonant first, vowel second. Every syllable, always.

slides.heading: Read it
body: A rice field.

slides.prompt: Build it yourself: the letter whose second loop lands on the right, followed by the long vowel. Say the syllable aloud — flat and level — and say what it means.

answers: Flat, mid tone. No rise, no fall.

slides.heading: Change the front, keep the back
body: The horse's letter, then the same long vowel. It means **to come**.
The word for **horse** is the same letters again — only the *tone* differs.
Say one flat when it should not be, and you have said the other.
The mark that writes that difference is coming.

slides.heading: Read it
body: To come.

slides.prompt: Take the word for a rice field and swap its first letter for the one whose loops stack down the left. Say the new syllable aloud, and say what it means.

slides.heading: Close the syllable
body: The mouse's letter, the long vowel, then the mouse's letter again.
It means **a long time** — what the net-mender waited, with **none** of her knots left.
One consonant can both **open** and **close** a syllable. Position decides.

slides.heading: Read it
body: A long time.

slides.prompt: Put the mouse's letter on both ends of the long vowel. Say the syllable aloud, close the ending cleanly, and say what it means.

slides.heading: Where that leaves you
body: Two consonants and one vowel gave you three words.
Stroke order, the head, the clockwise default, and the naming pattern.
Next: three more harbour letters, and why they all sound flat.
